newsitem.title: ITALY: Analysts wonder who is steering Olivetti.
newsitem.headline: Analysts wonder who is steering Olivetti.

text.p: One week after Carlo De Benedetti resigned as chairman of crisis-hit Olivetti, analysts on Wednesday pondered whether he, as its largest shareholder, or chief executive Francesco Caio is actually running the company.

In a series of high-level meetings, De Benedetti met with Italian Prime Minister Romano Prodi on Tuesday to discuss the Olivetti situation, while Caio meets Industry Minister Pierluigi Bersani and Labour Minister Tiziano Treu later on Wednesday.

Analysts said although De Benedetti stood down last week, his family holding group CIR is still the group's largest shareholder with an almost 15 percent stake, while the company's board contains De Benedetti's family and friends.
"Caio is meant to be in charge, so why was De Benedetti meeting Prodi? This a problem that is likely to haunt Caio for some time," said one Milan-based industry analyst.

The prime minister's office was quick to point out that discussions had not involved state aid for the ailing hi-tech group, but the talks only served to deepen the mystery of who is really in command at the loss-making company.

An Olivetti spokeswoman confirmed that the group had replied to the seven questions put to it by stock market watchdog authority Consob on the group's finances, but it is unlikely the questions or answers will be immediately made public.

Olivetti's problems reached crisis point last Tuesday when it reported first-half 1996 figures showing continued losses, deeper debts and falling sales. The next day, Renzo Francesconi, its director-general in charge of finance and auditing, resigned expressing his doubts over the clarity of the group's accounts.

His remarks led to Olivetti's shares being suspended on Thursday and Friday and then going into almost free fall on Monday and Tuesday, losing nearly 20 percent on Monday and almost six percent Tuesday to hit a record low of 555 lire.

Olivetti shares steadied Wednesday, up 3.03 percent at 585 lire at 1340 GMT, but they were still a long way off the 1,000 lire nominal level at which De Benedetti launched his record 2.257 trillion lire ($1.4 billion) rights issue late last year.

But the mounting crisis is not yet worrying the chairman of Italy's top deal-making merchant bank Mediobanca, as Francesco Cingano said no meetings between Olivetti and its creditor banks were planned.

For Caio his timetable is cluttered with meetings, Thursday sees him at the Senate Industry Commission, while he is set to meet Consob head Enzo Berlanda at the end of the week and then explain the group's strategy finances to analysts next week.

For many analysts, the meetings in Milan next Monday and London on Tuesday will seek to shed some light on the group's strategy and financial accounts, and also who is really pulling the strings at the top of Olivetti.
"Clearly, we will need some clarification on the group's accounting, strategy and disposals," said one London analyst.

Analysts said they would need information on what Consob's seven queries had focused upon and confirmation of the true debt level in the company. On strategy, whether the focus was still on telecoms and what De Benedetti's role now was, and finally on disposals -- what was for sale or for flotation.

They pointed out that De Benedetti's family lawyer Antonio Tesone had taken over as chairman and one of De Benedetti's sons Rodolfo is still on the board while another son Marco is still deeply involved in the company.
"De Benedetti has gone, but he is still there in spirit, one hopes that the operating function is with Caio, but one can never be sure with Olivetti," said another Milan analyst. ($1=1,522 lire)
